grades.excerpt: Intention I is the stable identity; records are attempts under it. Event endA ends record A with outcome failed and creates a pending response owned by steward. The response carries the intention id copied from records.A.intention. Event next consumes that response (state pending -> resolved) and creates record C whose intention is copied from responses.endA.intention. So continuation is a chain records.A.intention -> responses.endA.intention -> records.C.intention; C is a new record, not a resumption of A, and A's failed outcome persists. The chooser role is supplied by the event argument 'role' and checked against config.next_work_roles and the response owner; the engine does not authenticate who emitted the event. Model assessment (not observed): choose-subsequent-work has no guard on intentions.I.state or intentions.I.valid, so the rules would allow continuation under a closed or invalid intention.
grades.explanation: Explicitly identifies continuing I, failed historical A and new linked C; the record failure does not close the intention. Distinguishes untested model assessments from observed receipt states.

grades.excerpt: Blockage is not terminal: record A keeps its identity and null outcome, its lifecycle flips to blocked, and a pending response is created owned by orchestrator (contrast: end creates a steward-owned response). Recovery resolves that response and returns the same record to running; no continuation record is created. Model assessment: the recovery rule only guards the response owner. It does not require records[record].lifecycle == blocked, responses[response].state == pending, or responses[response].record == record, so as authored it could 'recover' an unrelated record or re-resolve an already resolved response. That is a rule gap, not an observed behavior.
grades.explanation: Uses first/second receipt states to distinguish blocked orchestrator-owned recovery from the steward terminal handoff. Same record recovers, no replacement created.

grades.excerpt: Terminal failure of a record is recorded as lifecycle ended plus outcome failed, and it is handled identically to success: one terminal-result rule, one steward-owned pending response. Failure of a record does not fail or close the intention; intentions.I stays open and valid, and record B continues running. The outcome value is stored but never consulted by any rule, so the model records terminal failure without giving it distinct consequences. Model assessment: the not_equals ended guard means a blocked record could be ended directly; whether that is intended is not stated in the data.
grades.explanation: Separates lifecycle ended, outcome failed, still-open I and steward response owner; it does not equate failed attempt with satisfied concern.

grades.excerpt: Two records under the same intention both end succeeded, each producing its own steward-owned response. Only endA was considered, so responses.endB remains pending work and intention I stays open; the model has no rule that closes an intention or reconciles two completions. grades.excerpt: Both interfaces submitted an answer against revision 0. The first (chat) applied and set the answer; the second (desk) was rejected before any rule ran because its expected revision was stale. Had it carried no expect_revision it would still have been rejected, this time by the guard answer == null with reason no-enabled-rule. Either way the first-arriving answer wins and the state is untouched by the loser, so ordering, not interface, decides the outcome. The authored rule also moves the decision owner from operator to orchestrator upon answering; the data does not say what that transfer means. grades.excerpt: The roles table separates who starts an agent from what drives its later actions. Assistant and architect are user-started and user-driven; orchestrator is user-started but autonomous afterwards; steward is started by an event and runs autonomously. The roles scenario is static: it replays no events and so demonstrates only the declared table. Nothing in the rules enforces start or drive; the only runtime use of roles is an existence check in choose-subsequent-work. The launch/drive distinction is therefore authored documentation inside the state, and the continuation run is merely consistent with it.
grades.explanation: Names the four declared start/drive pairs and explicitly notes these are configuration data, not enforced agent scheduling in this replay.
